findings.description: F003 declares a pure reconcile(registry, observed_canonical, now, policy) function, while F004 only says it loads observed canonical repos. No proposed feature pins the ledger-to-observed_canonical adapter that reads invocations.jsonl, ignores records without canonical_repo, aggregates count and max last_seen by canonical_repo_key, preserves scrubbed display, and proves command is never read.

F004 mixes two incompatible output expectations: JSON must contain scrubbed display plus counts only with no raw home path, but the tests also require a home-substituted projects add suggestion. If that suggestion appears in --json, C1 and the completion test fail; if it is human-only, the modality boundary is not pinned.

D010 says the durable DontPanic checkout was already registered, but the journey expects the p2a/p2-lock/main fixture to yield one used_unregistered candidate. Correct reconciliation would classify that same canonical repo as registered_active when the D010 registry state is present.

F002 requires refusing any canonical mapping that cannot be confirmed, but the evidence contract does not define deterministic confirmation rules once temp worktrees are gone. Implementers could either guess from scrubbed evidence or over-skip valid historical rows, breaking the required one-time backfill.

F002 acceptance says the local evidence file is excluded or ignored, but the steps do not name the ignore mechanism. Because DONTPANIC_HOME can be overridden during tests or local development, relying on ~/.dontpanic being outside the repo is weaker than the promised commit guard.

F002 validates that a reconstructed evidence path recomputes to the same path_key, but it does not explicitly reject or normalize a literal path_display that is actually under Path.home(). Such evidence could stamp a raw home path into historical canonical_repo data, and F003/F004 would then preserve or serialize it, violating the C1 privacy boundary.

F003 describes reconcile() as a pure function, but its steps also require registered-side keys to be computed via the F001 filesystem/git canonicalization. That creates an unresolved boundary: registered_active and registered_path_missing need canonical keys and path-existence facts, but the pure reconciliation input contract does not define where those facts come from.

The plan requires a minimum recency and count threshold, but the default policy values, timestamp field, boundary inclusivity, and CLI default wiring are not pinned. The isolated p2a/p2-lock/main fixture can only deterministically produce exactly one candidate if these policy cells are fixed before implementation.

F002 says a temp-prefix path must never be written as a canonical recommendation source, but the deterministic C4 skip matrix does not explicitly include a reconstructed canonical path under /tmp, /private/tmp, or /var/folders, nor an evidence row that marks such a path durable_checkout=true.

F002 promises a command or script with --dry-run, but the operator-facing entrypoint, ledger path resolution, DONTPANIC_HOME override behavior, exit codes, and dry-run/report schema are not specified. That leaves the backfill journey hard to test and ambiguous for the operator running the one-time migration.

F003 says missing registry paths emit path_exists=false with no canonical_repo_key, while reconcile is required to return registered_path_missing keyed on canonical_repo_key. That is an impossible key contract for the missing-path state and leaves F004 JSON shape ambiguous.

F001 only preserves canonical_repo through compact_ledger, but F003's C5 threshold depends on observed_count. Ledger compaction collapses duplicate invocation records without retaining a count, and F003 refers to summing observed_count on records that may not carry that field, so compacted ledgers can undercount usage and make min_count nondeterministic.

The completion test expects a canonical 'dontpanic' candidate and human output may print dontpanic projects add <name> <path>, but F003/F004 do not pin how an unregistered candidate gets a safe project name. Rows have scrubbed display and keys, while registry names must satisfy the project-name pattern.

F002 says to define the evidence-file contract from an already captured shape, but the proposed locked plan still does not spell out an exact JSON schema for canonical_repo entries and observation_path_key_to_canonical values. The C4 skip matrix depends on detecting multiple canonical keys and malformed fields deterministically.

The plan does not pin the classification matrix for registered_active versus registered_stale. F003 carries registry active, observed_count, and last_seen, but it never states whether registered_active means registry-active, recently observed above C5 thresholds, or both, nor how inactive registered rows, missing observations, low-count observations, or invalid timestamps classify.

Compaction invariance is asserted, but the mixed-attribution case is not pinned. If one bucket contains rows with canonical_repo and rows without canonical_repo, summing all rows into one compacted record can either inflate canonical observed_count or drop attribution depending on which row is preserved.

F002 rewrites invocations.jsonl atomically with a temp-file rename, but the plan does not coordinate that rewrite with the existing ledger writer's flock-based append path. A concurrent invocation during backfill could be appended to the old file handle and then lost by the rename.

The C4 matrix requires origin_key conflicts to skip, but the evidence schema is a canonical_repos map keyed by unique canonical path key, so the plan does not define what value can conflict with what during backfill of records that lack canonical_repo.

C7 and the non-goals exclude git-hook behavior, but none of the proposed feature acceptances add a negative guard around the projects CLI changes. F004 and F005 will edit the same command surface where hook-related behavior could accidentally reappear.

The F006/F002 backfill evidence contract validates allowed field names but does not pin required canonical_repo field presence, value types, durable_checkout semantics, or an origin_key hash/no-secret shape before copying origin_key into the ledger. A malformed evidence object could therefore stamp an incomplete canonical_repo or persist a raw origin-shaped value despite the C1/C4 privacy boundary.

F003 introduces registered_canonical.canonicalization_status, but the reconcile contract does not define what happens when a registered path exists yet canonicalization cannot produce a canonical_repo_key. The C5 table says existing registered paths become registered_stale or registered_active, while the projection also says non-missing rows are keyed by canonical_repo_key, leaving this failure cell unclassified.

The journey acceptance requires --dry-run to report would-stamp, would-skip, and already-stamped counts, but the pinned C4 report schema uses would_stamp as a count while would_skip is a list of skipped row objects. That mismatch leaves operator-facing status and tests ambiguous before implementation locks.

F006 validates durable_checkout only as a boolean and F002 copies it from evidence, but once the reconstructed canonical path is confirmed non-temp, C3 implies durable_checkout must be true. The plan rejects durable_checkout=true for a temp canonical path, but does not reject or recompute durable_checkout=false for a confirmed durable canonical, which could stamp records that F003 later skips.

F004 says discover --json emits scrubbed display, keys, counts, recency, suggestion status, and suggested_name, but neither F003 nor F004 pins the exact JSON field names, value types, or suggestion_status enum. That leaves the completion test and downstream metadata substrate open to incompatible interpretations.

F002 says the backfill engine holds the live writer ledger lock, while F005 says the entrypoint acquires the same lock across the F002 sequence. Without a single pinned lock owner or reentrant transaction API, implementation can double-acquire a non-reentrant lock or accidentally run part of validation outside the critical section.
